steps.html:
Hipsters reject anything mainstream, which includes the word hipster. A trend-spotter tries to describe them for seven minutes and ends up saying kind of, sort of and and stuff like that about forty times — which turns out to be the interesting part.

  • Recognise vague language and hear what it is doing
  • Follow a long interview about a subculture
  • Build and use compound adjectives
  • Write a description of a group of people

steps.title: What speakers say when they do not want to be exact
steps.html:
Read this before the recordings. It is very common, and it is not sloppiness.

Spoken English is full of vague expressions, and they are doing two different jobs.

When the speaker cannot find the precise word: kind of, sort of, a bit, something like. His beard is a sort of orange colour. The speaker knows the colour and does not have a name for it.

When there are more items in the list: and so on, and that kind of thing, and stuff like that, or whatever, and places like that. The shop sells vintage clothes, records and that kind of thing.

Recognising these matters for two reasons. First, they are unstressed and very fast, so they can swallow the words around them. Second, they tell you the speaker has finished the list — you do not need to wait for more.

In writing they are usually a weakness. In speech they are normal, and a speaker who never uses them sounds like a document.

steps.title: What does 'and stuff like that' tell you?
options: The speaker has lost their place.
The list could go on, and the speaker is closing it.
The speaker is unsure whether the items are correct.
steps.answer: The list could go on, and the speaker is closing it.
steps.why: It is a list-closing signal, and once you hear it you can stop waiting for more items.

steps.why: Whatever the label happens to be at the time.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The interviewee explains that hipsters reject mainstream culture and also that they do not want to be labelled hipsters.
steps.prompt: What difficulty does that create for the interview itself?
options: None — the two statements are unrelated.
The people being described would reject the description, so the category exists mainly for the people outside it.
It shows the interviewee has misunderstood the subculture.
steps.answer: The people being described would reject the description, so the category exists mainly for the people outside it.
steps.why: He says as much: the label is applied from outside. Everything after that in the interview is a description nobody in it would accept.

steps.title: Two words, one hyphen, one adjective
steps.html:
How they are built, and how they behave.

A compound adjective is two or more words working as one adjective before a noun. They are built from a small number of patterns.

adjective / adverb + past participle: clean-shaven, well-known, little-known, tight-fitting... and thick-rimmed, run-down, second-hand.

noun + past participle: floral-patterned, hand-made, home-made, sun-dried.

adjective + present participle: tight-fitting, good-looking, long-lasting, hard-working.

noun / prefix + adjective: eco-friendly, user-friendly, high-tech, low-tech, world-famous.

Two rules of use. They take the hyphen before a noun and often lose it after the verb: a well-known band but the band is well known. And the first element never takes a plural or a comparative: a five-year-old child, not a five-years-old child; a two-hour meeting, not a two-hours meeting.

steps.title: Turning a phrase into a compound adjective
steps.html:
1. Start with the full phrase: glasses with thick rims.
  2. Move the description in front of the noun and join it: thick-rimmed glasses. The noun rims becomes the past participle rimmed, and it loses its plural.
  3. The same move works elsewhere: a dress with a floral pattern → a floral-patterned dress. A bike with a fixed wheel → a fixed-wheel bike.
  4. Watch the number rule: a child who is five years old → a five-year-old child. Singular, always.
  5. And after the verb the hyphen usually disappears: the glasses were thick rimmed, the band is well known.

steps.title: You are going to describe a group of people.

options.label: A subculture you can recognise where you live
A group you belonged to when you were younger
A group everybody labels and nobody in it accepts the label

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least five compound adjectives, and at least two vague expressions where a written list would be too long.
steps.html:
• Open with what you can see from a distance, using compound adjectives.
  • Say who they are, closing the list with a vague expression.
  • Say what is true underneath the stereotype.
  • Close with a second conditional about the label.

Useful language

  • The stereotype is easy to draw: … , … and that kind of thing.
  • They wear tight-fitting / retro-style / second-hand …
  • They prefer low-tech objects: record players, typewriters and so on.
  • What they reject hardest is the label itself.
  • They're kind of anti anything that's …
  • If you called one of them a … , they would deny it.
steps.modelHtml:
The ones outside the coffee place on Gogol Street

You can identify them from about forty metres. Tight-fitting jeans, thick-rimmed glasses, a retro-style shirt that was probably second-hand, and a bicycle with one gear leaning against a wall that nobody has repainted in twenty years.

They are all in their late twenties, they all work in design or media or publishing or that kind of thing, and they are all faintly embarrassed to be recognisable at all.

What is easy to miss is that most of the stereotype is true and none of it is the point. They mend things. They buy eco-friendly products and second-hand furniture and home-made bread, and they were doing all of that before the area became fashionable.

If you called any of them a hipster, they would deny it, and they would be kind of right.
